title: How to Fix a Dripping Faucet

seo.title: How to Fix a Dripping Faucet
seo.meta_description: To fix a dripping faucet, identify the faucet type, shut off water, and replace the correct wear part without damaging finishes or supply connections.
seo.search_intent: Repair a dripping faucet by determining whether the cartridge, washer, disk, or seat is leaking and knowing when corrosion or supply leaks require escalation.

excerpt: A drip from the spout usually points to a worn shutoff component; water around the handle or under the sink points somewhere else. Locating the leak first prevents unnecessary disassembly.
content_html:
Before buying a washer, find exactly where the water is escaping. A spout drip, a leak around the handle, and water at a supply connection under the sink are different repairs.

Identify the faucet mechanism

Many modern faucets use cartridges; others use ceramic disks, ball assemblies, or compression stems. Find the brand and model when possible because replacement parts must match.

Shut off water and verify it is actually off

Close the fixture stops under the sink and open the faucet to relieve pressure. If a stop valve will not shut off or begins leaking when moved, do not force it repeatedly; the main shutoff or professional help may be needed.

Protect the finish while disassembling

Cover the drain so small screws cannot disappear and use tools that will not scar chrome or plated finishes. Photograph layers or place parts in order as they come off.

Replace the wear part that matches the design

A cartridge faucet may need a cartridge or seals. A compression faucet may need a washer or attention to its valve seat. Use only plumbing-compatible lubricant where the manufacturer calls for it.

Restore water slowly and inspect two areas

Check the spout first, then every connection you disturbed under the sink. A repair that stops the drip but leaves a cabinet leak is not complete.

If parts are badly corroded, the shutoff valve does not work, or the faucet body itself is cracked, replacing the fixture or calling a plumber can be more reliable than further disassembly.

faq.question: Do I have to turn off the water first?
faq.answer: Yes. Close the fixture stops and verify that flow has stopped before taking the faucet apart.

faq.question: Why does it still drip after a new washer?
faq.answer: The faucet may use a different mechanism, the valve seat may be worn, or the entire cartridge may need replacement.

faq.question: When should I replace the whole faucet?
faq.answer: A cracked body, severe corrosion, unavailable parts, or leaks in several areas can make full replacement the better repair.
